classification.difficultyReason: Construct a diagram and prove the angle in a semicircle using equal radii, isosceles base angles and exterior angles.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Construct a large circle with centre $O$ and draw a diameter $AOB$.

answer.short: A circle centred at $O$, with $A$ and $B$ on the circle and $AB$ passing through $O$.
answer.worked: Use compasses to draw a large circle centred at $O$. Draw a straight line through $O$ and label its intersections with the circle $A$ and $B$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Choose any point $P$, different from $A$ and $B$, on the circle and join $PA$ and $PB$.

answer.short: A point $P$ on the circle, distinct from $A$ and $B$, joined to both endpoints of the diameter.
answer.worked: Mark $P$ anywhere on the circle except at $A$ or $B$. Draw the chords $PA$ and $PB$ on the construction from part a.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Prove that $\angle APB$ is a right angle. Do this by drawing the radius $OP$ and working with the angles in the two isosceles triangles $AOP$ and $BOP$.

answer.short:
$\angle APB=90^{\circ}$.

Equal radii give two isosceles triangles. Their exterior angles at $O$ are twice the corresponding angles at $P$ and together form a straight angle.
answer.worked:
Draw $OP$. Since $OA=OP=OB$ are radii, $\triangle AOP$ and $\triangle BOP$ are isosceles. Thus $\angle OAP=\angle APO$ and $\angle OBP=\angle BPO$.

Using exterior angles at $O$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle POB&=\angle OAP+\angle APO\\\angle POB&=2\angle APO\\\angle POA&=\angle OBP+\angle BPO\\\angle POA&=2\angle BPO.\end{align*}$$
Since $A$, $O$ and $B$ lie on a straight line,
$$\begin{align*}\angle APB&=\angle APO+\angle BPO\\\angle APB&=\tfrac12(\angle POB+\angle POA)\\\angle APB&=\tfrac12\times180^{\circ}\\\angle APB&=90^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: An authored example of the requested student construction: circle, diameter AOB, arbitrary circumference point P, chords PA and PB, and radius OP. No supplied source figure exists.
spec.mathematics: OA=OB=OP; A, O and B are collinear; P lies on the circle and differs from A and B. The chosen orientation is illustrative and imposes no numerical angle or length.
